title: Kitchen Installation Cost UK: Full Price Breakdown
description: Kitchen installation cost UK explained, including units, labour, plumbing, electrics and finishing work, with practical tips for comparing quotes.

blocks.text: If you are budgeting for a new kitchen, the installation cost can be difficult to judge from online prices alone. A flat-pack kitchen may appear affordable, but the final bill can also include cabinet assembly, worktop fitting, plumbing, electrics, flooring, tiling, decorating and waste removal. As a rough guide, a straightforward UK kitchen installation may typically cost around £3,000 to £7,000 for labour and associated work, excluding the kitchen itself. A larger or more complex project can take the overall budget well beyond £15,000. Every project is different, so the most useful figure is based on your room, chosen materials and the extent of the changes; request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.
What is included in kitchen installation cost?

The phrase kitchen installation covers more than putting units in place. A typical quote may include removing the existing kitchen, preparing the room, assembling and securing cabinets, fitting doors and drawers, installing worktops, connecting appliances and carrying out final adjustments. If the layout changes, the work may also involve moving water and waste pipes, altering electrical circuits, adding lighting or repairing walls and floors. Ask whether prices include VAT, delivery, disposal of the old kitchen and making good after the trades have finished. These details can make two apparently similar quotes differ significantly.

items: Kitchen units and panels: as a rough guide, typically £1,500 to £8,000 or more, depending on size, supplier, specification and whether the units are flat-pack, rigid or bespoke.
Worktops: as a rough guide, typically £500 to £4,000, with laminate usually at the lower end and natural stone, quartz or other premium materials costing more.
Installation labour: as a rough guide, typically £2,000 to £6,000 for a standard room, although complicated layouts, large kitchens and extensive preparation can increase this.
Removal and disposal: as a rough guide, this may typically cost several hundred pounds, depending on the amount of cabinetry, appliances and waste.

Appliances, sink and taps: as a rough guide, typically from around £1,000 for a basic selection, with integrated, premium or multiple appliances increasing the total. Every project differs, so request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.

Typical labour costs for fitting a kitchen

Labour is often quoted as a fixed project price rather than a simple daily rate. This can be helpful because the cost is linked to the agreed scope, but the quote should still explain what the labour covers. Cabinet installation, worktop cutting, appliance integration and final adjustments each require different levels of time and care. A small replacement kitchen with the same layout may take considerably less work than a renovation involving new flooring, wall repairs and relocated services. If the installer needs to return after another contractor, that may also affect the programme and cost.

items: Plumbing: as a rough guide, typically £300 to £1,500 for connecting or relocating a sink, dishwasher, washing machine and other water-fed appliances. Moving pipework further across the room can add preparation and repair work.

Electrical work: as a rough guide, a modest installation may typically cost around £500 to £2,000, while additional sockets, new lighting, an appliance circuit or wider alterations can increase the figure.
Gas appliance connections: if a gas hob or cooker is involved, confirm exactly what is included and use an appropriately qualified professional for that work.

Making good: chasing walls, repairing plaster, filling gaps and repainting after services have moved may be priced separately. Every project differs, so request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.

blocks.text: How the kitchen itself affects the price

The number of units is only one part of the calculation. A simple single-wall kitchen generally needs less worktop, fewer corner cabinets and less installation time than a U-shaped design with an island. Tall housings, deep drawers, larder units, internal storage, bespoke panels and integrated appliances also add materials and fitting time. Worktop material is another major choice: laminate is usually the most economical, while timber, quartz, granite and other solid surfaces require different fabrication and installation arrangements. Handles, hinges, drawer runners and cabinet interiors can all affect the final specification.
Finishing work that is easy to overlook

items: Flooring, skirting boards and threshold adjustments
Wall tiling or a splashback, including adhesive, grout and trims
Plaster repairs and preparation around removed cabinets
Painting and decorating, particularly where the old layout has left exposed or uneven areas
Lighting, extractor installation and finishing around sockets
Delivery, protection of existing areas, cleaning and removal of packaging

blocks.text: How to compare kitchen installation quotes fairly

The cheapest quote is not necessarily the lowest final cost. Start by giving each contractor the same plans, appliance list and specification, then compare the detail line by line. Look for allowances described as provisional sums, because the eventual price may change when the exact material or amount of work is known. Confirm whether the quote covers removal, waste, delivery, worktop templating and cut-outs, appliance connections, plumbing alterations, electrics, tiling, flooring and decorating. It is also sensible to ask how variations will be priced and approved before extra work begins.

Ways to keep installation costs under control

items: Keep the sink, dishwasher and cooker close to their existing positions if the current layout works well.
Choose the kitchen and appliances before final pricing, rather than relying on broad allowances.
Use standard cabinet sizes where possible; unusual dimensions often require infill panels or bespoke work.
Decide early whether you need new flooring, tiling, lighting or decorating so these costs are not added unexpectedly.
Keep a contingency in the budget for hidden problems such as damaged walls, uneven floors or outdated services.
Request a written scope of work, payment schedule and variation process before work starts.

faq.q: How much does a kitchen installation cost in the UK?
faq.a: As a rough guide, labour and associated installation work may typically cost around £3,000 to £7,000, excluding the kitchen itself. Larger or more complex projects can cost considerably more. Every project differs, so request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.

faq.q: How much does it cost to fit a kitchen without buying the units?
faq.a: As a rough guide, a standard installation may typically cost roughly £2,000 to £6,000 for labour, depending on the room size, layout, worktops, appliances and whether plumbing or electrical work is needed. Every project differs, so request a free, no-obligation quote for accurate pricing.

faq.q: Is plumbing included in a kitchen fitting quote?
faq.a: Not always. Some quotes include basic connections, while others price plumbing separately. Confirm whether the quote covers moving pipes, connecting appliances, waste disposal and making good.

faq.q: How can I compare kitchen fitter quotes?
faq.a: Give each installer the same specification and compare the written scope, VAT, labour, materials, waste removal, appliance connections, finishing work, exclusions and variation process.

faq.q: What is the most expensive part of a kitchen installation?
faq.a: The largest costs are often the kitchen units and worktops, followed by labour. Relocating plumbing or electrics, premium appliances and extensive flooring or decorating can also have a substantial effect.
